rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Conduction:** Heat transfer through a material without any bulk motion of the material itself. Energy is transferred from molecule to molecule via collisions and lattice vibrations (phonons). In metals, free electrons also carry thermal energy, making conduction highly efficient.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Thermal conductivity depends on the thickness of the material. ✅ $k$ is a MATERIAL PROPERTY — it does not depend on dimensions. Thickness affects heat flow rate, but not $k$. A thicker copper bar has the same $k$ as a thin one.  ·  ❌ Metals feel cold because they are at a lower temperature. ✅ Metals feel cold because they CONDUCT heat away from your hand faster. At the same temperature, metal and wood feel different because of different $k$ values.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Joseph Fourier developed the mathematical theory of heat conduction in 1822, introducing the concept of thermal conductivity and the partial differential equation that bears his name — the heat equation.  ·  Diamond has the highest thermal conductivity of any known bulk material at room temperature (~2200 W/(m·K)), exceeding copper (~400 W/(m·K)). This is because of its rigid crystal lattice and strong covalent bonds.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Fourier's law of heat conduction:** The rate of heat flow through a material is given by $H = \frac{Q}{t} = kA\frac{T_1 - T_2}{L}$, where $k$ is the thermal conductivity, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $T_1 - T_2$ is the temperature difference, and $L$ is the length. In differential form: $H = -kA\frac{dT}{dx}$. The negative sign ensures heat flows from hot to cold.  ·  **Thermal conductivity $k$:** A material property that quantifies how well a material conducts heat. Units: $\text{W/(m·K)}$. Metals have high $k$ (copper: ~400 W/(m·K)), insulators have low $k$ (wood: ~0.1 W/(m·K)), and gases have very low $k$ (air: ~0.025 W/(m·K)).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Superfluid helium (He-4 below 2.17 K) has an extraordinarily high thermal conductivity — millions of times greater than ordinary helium — because of quantum mechanical effects in the superfluid state.  ·  In building construction, the thermal resistance (R-value) of insulation is a critical specification. Higher R-values mean better insulation. A typical wall requires R-13 to R-21, while attics need R-30 to R-60.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: ❌ Heat flows from hot to cold, so Fourier's law has no negative sign. ✅ The negative sign in $H = -kA\frac{dT}{dx}$ ensures heat flows from high temperature to low temperature. Without it, heat would flow from cold to hot.  ·  ❌ A good conductor of heat is a good insulator. ✅ Opposite! A good conductor ($k$ large) conducts heat well and is a poor insulator. A good insulator ($k$ small) conducts heat poorly.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Why metals conduct heat well:** In metals, free electrons are mobile and can move rapidly through the lattice, colliding with ions and carrying energy. These free electrons act as efficient energy carriers, giving metals their high thermal conductivity.  ·  **Fayer's apparatus:** Used to measure thermal conductivity of liquids. A steam jacket surrounds the liquid-filled cylinder. Thermometers at known distances measure the temperature gradient. By measuring the heat flow and temperature difference, $k$ can be calculated.  ·  **Temperature dependence of $k$:** For metals, $k$ DECREASES with increasing temperature because lattice vibrations scatter electrons more frequently. For non-metals and gases, $k$ generally INCREASES with temperature as molecular motion increases.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The rate of heat flow is the same as the temperature. ✅ Heat flow rate ($H$, in Watts) and temperature (in Kelvin) are completely different quantities. A large temperature difference across a small resistance gives high heat flow.  ·  ❌ Fourier's law applies only to steady-state conditions. ✅ Fourier's law applies at every instant — both steady state and transient conditions. The differential form $H = -kA\frac{dT}{dx}$ holds at each point in time.  ·  ❌ Air is a good conductor of heat. ✅ Air is a poor conductor ($k \approx 0.025$ W/(m·K)). However, air is an excellent convective medium — convection dominates heat transfer in air, not conduction.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A copper rod ($k = 400$ W/(m·K)) of length 0.5 m and cross-section 0.01 m² has ends at 100°C and 0°C. Find the heat flow rate. $H = kA\frac{\Delta T}{L} = 400 \times 0.01 \times \frac{100}{0.5} = 800$ W. Heat flows at 800 J/s from hot to cold end.  ·  A wall consists of a 10 cm brick layer ($k = 0.7$ W/(m·K)) followed by a 5 cm insulation layer ($k = 0.04$ W/(m·K)). Inside temperature is 25°C, outside is 5°C. Find heat flow per unit area. $R_{total} = \frac{0.1}{0.7} + \frac{0.05}{0.04} = 0.143 + 1.25 = 1.393$ m²K/W. $H/A = \frac{20}{1.393} = 14.4$ W/m².  ·  A rectangular slab has dimensions 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm. Heat flows along the 20 cm direction with a temperature difference of 100°C. If $k = 0.5$ W/(m·K), find the heat flow rate. Area $A = 10 \times 5 = 50$ cm² = $5 \times 10^{-3}$ m². $H = 0.5 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{100}{0.2} = 1.25$ W.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Thermal resistance:** Analogous to electrical resistance. $R_{th} = \frac{L}{kA}$. The heat flow equation becomes $H = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{th}}$, directly analogous to Ohm's law $I = \frac{V}{R}$. For composite walls, resistances add: $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + ...$  ·  **Thermal conductivity vs. temperature gradient:** The heat flow depends on the TEMPERATURE GRADIENT ($\Delta T / L$), not just the temperature difference. A large $\Delta T$ across a thick slab may produce less heat flow than a small $\Delta T$ across a thin slab.  ·  **Application — building insulation:** Double-glazed windows use an air gap ($k_{air} \approx 0.025$) between glass panes. The air gap provides high thermal resistance. Adding argon gas (even lower $k$) further reduces heat transfer.
